prayer.text: Blessed Fulton J. Sheen, pray for us.

cues.text: A Farm Boy Called Fulton
On May 8, 1895, in El Paso, Illinois, a boy named Peter John Sheen was born, the eldest of four sons of Newton and Delia Sheen.
As a young boy he came to be known by his mother's maiden name, Fulton, and the name would one day be known around the world.
After his baptism, Delia dedicated him to the Blessed Virgin Mary , and he renewed that dedication himself at his First Communion.
In 1900 the family moved to Peoria so that he could attend the cathedral school, and he often served Mass there for Bishop Spalding.
A Promise at the Altar
Sheen attended Spalding Institute and St. Viator's College, and then he entered St. Paul Seminary in Minnesota.
On September 20, 1919, he was ordained a priest of the Diocese of Peoria at St. Mary's Cathedral.
On that day he made a promise to make a Holy Hour before the Blessed Sacrament every day, and he kept it for the rest of his life.
In Chicago one evening, a pastor let him into a locked church for his hour and then forgot him.
Two hours later Sheen escaped through a small window and landed in a coal bin.
The Scholar and the Voice
Sheen's mind was as formidable as his faith.
After ordination he studied at the Catholic University in Washington and at Louvain in Belgium, where in 1923 he earned a doctorate in philosophy.
That same year he became the first American to win the Cardinal Mercier Prize for International Philosophy.
He also attended classes at the Sorbonne in Paris and the Angelicum in Rome.
After nine months at St. Patrick's, an inner-city parish in Peoria, he began teaching in 1926 at the Catholic University in Washington, where he remained until 1950.
In 1930 he started a weekly Sunday-night radio program, The Catholic Hour, which reportedly drew about four million listeners a week for two decades.
Then he moved to television with Life Is Worth Living, which ran until 1957.
The show was unpaid and unscripted and aired on Tuesday evenings.
At first only three stations carried it, but after a national magazine feature the number jumped to fifteen in under two months.
At its height it drew an estimated thirty million viewers a week.
In 1953 Sheen won an Emmy Award for Most Outstanding Television Personality.
He credited the four Gospel writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
Missions, a Council, and a Last Embrace
In 1950 Sheen became national director of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith in the United States, a post he held until 1966.
One estimate says he raised hundreds of millions of dollars for the missions.
At the beatification, Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle recalled that Sheen spent time among people with leprosy in Uganda.
Sheen was consecrated a bishop in Rome on June 11, 1951.
He attended every session of the Second Vatican Council , and years later Pope Benedict XVI told Bishop Daniel Jenky that he had known Sheen personally and worked with him there.
In 1966 Sheen became Bishop of Rochester, New York.
Three years later he resigned, insisting he was not retiring but "retreading," and Pope Paul VI named him titular archbishop of Newport in Wales.
On October 2, 1979, Pope John Paul II embraced him at St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York and called him a loyal son of the Church.
Sheen died on December 9, 1979, at age 84, in the chapel of his Manhattan apartment.
He was laid to rest in the cathedral crypt.
A Long Road to the Altar
Bishop Daniel Jenky of Peoria petitioned Rome to open Sheen's cause in September 2002, and Sheen became a Servant of God.
On June 28, 2012, Pope Benedict XVI recognized his heroic virtue and named him Venerable.
The miracle came from an infant.
In 2010 James Fulton Engstrom had no heartbeat or breath for 61 minutes after his birth, while his family prayed for Sheen's intercession.
Then the child's heart began to beat.
In 2014 the Vatican's medical experts judged the recovery beyond scientific explanation.
Then the cause stalled.
New York objected to moving Sheen's body to Peoria, but in 2019 the courts sided with his niece, and the body reached Peoria on June 27.
Pope Francis approved the miracle in July.

The Bishop of Rochester had asked the Vatican to examine how Sheen, as bishop there, handled two abusive priests.
In 2023 the Sheen Foundation reported that a New York law firm it hired found he had acted appropriately.
On February 9, 2026, Peoria announced that the Holy See had once again approved his beatification.
A Rare Day in St. Louis
On September 24, 2026, Sheen was beatified at The Dome at America's Center in St. Louis before an estimated 50,000 people.
Cardinal Tagle presided as the delegate of Pope Leo XIV .
He read the pope's apostolic letter in Latin, Bishop Louis Tylka of Peoria read it in English, and at that moment Sheen became Blessed.
Such a Mass is rare on American soil.
It was the first beatification in the United States since Michael McGivney's in October 2020, which COVID limits kept small.
Not since Solanus Casey in 2017 had thousands gathered for an American's beatification at home.

His feast day is December 9, the anniversary of his death.
What He Still Says
In his homily, Cardinal Tagle said Sheen was blessed not because he was famous but because of his communion with Jesus and with the poor.
That is a word for every believer.
Msgr. Jason Gray of the Sheen Foundation says the source of Sheen's preaching was his time in prayer before the Blessed Sacrament.
The microphone reached millions, but the quiet hour made the man.
Any of us can begin where he began, with a single hour before the Lord.
One more approved miracle is needed for canonization, and the cause is already studying six reported ones.
